title: Christmas in the Clouds
full_review:
No teepees and tomahawks, thank you. A largely Native American cast notwithstanding, this is basically an old-fashioned romantic comedy which, in its modest way, should help dispel misguided notions of that often stereotyped ethnic group.

"Christmas in the Clouds" (Slowhand Cinema/Majestic Films), which has been playing the festival circuit, concerns young widow Tina (Mariana Tosca), who, on a whim, travels from New York to Michigan to surprise her pen pal-suitor Joe (Sam Vlahos), whose sardonic narration amusingly opens and closes the film.

They've never met, and she doesn't know he's an elderly man, just as he assumes that, as a widow, she must be a mature matron.

When she arrives, Tina mistakes Joe's good-looking son, Ray (Tim Vahle), the tribe's ski resort owner who's emotionally shut down after a recent divorce, to be her correspondent, while Ray, in turn, mistakes her for an incognito hotel critic, there to size up the place for an influential travel guide.

The resort's guest roster also includes reliable character actor M. Emmet Walsh playing inebriated rotund Irish hotel guest Stu O'Malley (speaking of stereotypes), who has some family issues -- and a secret you'll easily guess -- of his own, and a lovely turn by British veteran Rosalind Ayres as gracious art-loving guest Mabel.

It doesn't take long for a mutual attraction to blossom between Ray and Tina, and they spend a night together. "This isn't the 19th century," says Tina.

The morning-after discussion between the two brings more serious misunderstandings, and later on it is discovered that Joe and Stu are missing during a snowstorm, which is paralleled by a subplot involving a child's missing mouse, a sweet if obvious touch.

All will be set right by the end, but Ray and Tina will experience a few more bumps before then.

The staff is a colorful bunch, including as it does front desk marketing gal Mary (Sheila Tousey), secretly enamored of romance novels, who mistakenly fingers Tina as the travel writer; vegetarian chef Earl (Graham Greene), who goes from table to table discouraging patrons from eating anything that once moved; handyman lothario Phil (Jonathan Joss); and assorted others.

Rita Coolidge, Wes Studi and Shirley Cheechoo round out the pleasing cast.

Triple-threat producer-writer-director Kate Montgomery's Sundance, Utah-shot film (only the second movie filmed there, after Robert Redford's "Jeremiah Johnson") has fashioned an agreeable, refreshingly offbeat tale -- the "first romantic comedy set in Indian Country," they claim -- if not quite in the zany Howard Hawks or Frank Capra mode as the publicity materials promise.

The pace is hardly in the screwball tradition, nor, to be picky about it, would Ray and Tina have slept together before marriage in a Hawks or Capra film! But with its quirky, gentle humor, this low-key story of love and forgiveness will make respectable holiday viewing.

This film contains a smattering of crude language, mild sexual humor and innuendo, a nongraphic bedroom scene, and a permissive view of premarital sex. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
